 From Malaysia and Singapore to Ho Chi Minh City, Haze Is Back in the Picture
 Haze overhangs the Ho Chi Minh City skyline. Photo by Andy Gough 
 By:
 Albert Nguyen
 October 26, 2026 ,
 9:50 AM 
 00:00 / 00:00 
 When haze descended on Malaysia and Singapore in October, the familiar complaints returned. Air quality warnings were issued, schools closed in parts of the region, and residents found their daily lives disrupted by smoke from fires in Indonesia. The ASEAN Specialized Meteorological Centre activated Alert Level 3, its highest warning, as the smoke spread across borders.
 The region has seen this cycle too many times: governments pledge to work together, investigations are announced, and then the issue slips down the agenda once the smoke disperses and daily life returns to normal. The underlying problem, however, remains — waiting to resurface with the next dry season.
 This year, the haze has also raised questions further east, in Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam’s largest metropolis, where grayish skies are hardly unusual. Heavy traffic and industrial activities on the city’s outskirts have long contributed to air pollution. But the shade has grown darker in recent weeks, prompting speculation about whether smoke from Indonesian forest fires has reached southern Vietnam.
 While scientists were trying to explain the phenomenon, Vietnamese netizens were making jokes about it.
 “Why are the graphics only 480p today, Saigon?” read a caption on Lang Thang Sài Gòn , a Facebook community page with more than one million followers. The caption compared the blurry Saigon skyline to a YouTube video struggling with a poor internet connection. And judging by the responses elsewhere on social media, the city's residents had plenty more to say about the unexpected visual effects.
 Under a post on Hóng Sài Gòn , a Facebook community page with around 1.3 million followers, sarcastic comments piled up. “Had me all excited for a second. I thought the Lunar New Year was coming early!” wrote a user named BZBigZero. Another user, Hồng Thư, offered some questionable health advice: “Breathe in! It's good for your lungs!” 
 The first joke likened the haze to the misty weather associated with the Vietnamese Lunar New Year. The second was a darker joke with a morbid twist. 
 On TikTok, commuters filmed Saigon’s high-rises fading into the haze, comparing the city’s skyline to the mist-shrouded city of Da Lat while reminding their viewers to put the masks on.
 Since mid-September, haze has partly obscured the city's highest buildings, including the iconic Landmark 81 and Bitexco Financial Tower. While some social media users have blamed the blurry skies on Indonesian forest fires, Vietnamese media explained that a clear connection would require more evidence.
 Indeed, Vietnam is no stranger to haze and smog. In Ho Chi Minh City, a clean-air assessment identified road transport and industrial activities as major sources of emissions, with construction and waste burning also contributing. A 2026 study of particulate pollution in the city similarly called out transport and fossil-fuel combustion as significant sources.
 The real challenge is making those responsible answer for the damage. That means looking beyond the fires to the commercial interests driving land clearing and whether authorities are willing to hold them to account, even when the resulting smoke crosses national borders. The consequences of inaction are not abstract.
 Speaking at the Global Tipping Points Conference in Kuala Lumpur, economist Kate Raworth pointed to how environmental damage becomes part of everyday urban life, with people witnessing “the consequences of inaction, like polluted air and rubbish in the river.”In Ho Chi Minh City, the haze has become difficult to overlook, even as residents turn it into an internet punchline.
 And while the internet can turn a hazy morning into a running joke, no amount of laughter can bring the city's skyline back into focus.
 Albert Nguyen is an essayist and reporter based in Ho Chi Minh City.
